name: Burning Lands
lines: Fumaroles: where the volcano breathes
A fumarole is an opening in the ground where volcanic gas and steam escape. Most of the plume is water vapour.
The gas carries sulphur. As it cools at the mouth, yellow sulphur crystals grow round the lip. Gather them here (look for the glow) for the Phoenix's nest and the smiths.
The rotten-egg smell is hydrogen sulphide gas. Real fumaroles can be dangerous: in the Burning Lands the keepers watch them for you.
Famous fumarole fields: Solfatara near Naples, Yellowstone in the United States, and the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes in Alaska.
Where the ground stays hot
Here the lava runs just under a thin crust, and the ground glows through the cracks.
Emberstone, the warm rock the smiths burn in the great forge, cools out of it. Gather it here (look for the glow) and take it to the smiths.
On Earth, ground this hot is found on fresh lava flows, as on Hawaii's Kīlauea, where a crust can be walked on by scientists in thick boots a few days after it forms.
Stay on the dark plates: the bright cracks are hotter than any oven.
Watching the river of fire
The watchers ring the bell if the lava rises. Real volcano observatories, like the one on Hawaii, watch with tiltmeters, gas sensors and seismometers.
Lava rivers move from a slow crawl to faster than you can run, depending on how runny the lava is and how steep the ground.
Cross only by the Ember Bridge and the Ash Bridge.
The travellers' stop
Water, bread and shade before the road to the Fire Palace.
Drink often in heat: a body loses water fast by sweating, even before you feel thirsty.
The cooks bake on hot stones, the oldest kind of oven there is.
Pyrrhos, warden of the gate
a fire elemental who guards the Fire Palace, warm-hearted though made of flame, proud of the palace and its hundred rooms
Ignatia, warden of the gate
a fire elemental who guards the Fire Palace beside Pyrrhos; she loves the palace's Lantern Room and tells visitors to light the lanterns there
Calder, keeper of the river
a fire elemental who walks the north bank of the lava river and keeps travellers to the bridges; it can stand in lava, you cannot
Scoria, keeper of the river
a fire elemental who walks the south bank of the lava river; it knows the lava's moods and tells real facts about lava and how it flows
Solfa, of the vents
a fire elemental who tends the Smoking Vents; it explains fumaroles, steam and sulphur, and asks gatherers to stand upwind
Brasa, of the ember beds
a fire elemental who tends the Ember Beds; it helps gatherers find emberstone and explains how lava crust forms
the captain of the Lava Watch, a weathered woman in a red heat-cloak who has watched the lava river for thirty years; she knows real volcano science and loves to share it
a young lava-watcher on his first season, keen and a little nervous, who has learned every fact about lava he can
the cook of Cinder Rest, who bakes flatbread on hot stones and makes everyone drink water before the road
a water-seller at Cinder Rest with clay jars of cool spring water from under the mountain, cheerful and full of travellers' gossip
an old storyteller who sits at Cinder Rest and tells the tales of fire from many lands: Prometheus, Pele, Agni, the firebird, truthfully saying which are myths
two travellers, a brother and sister, on their way to see the Phoenix rise; they have come a long way and are excited and a bit footsore
a pilgrim monk walking slowly to the Fire Palace to see the eternal flame; calm and kind, he talks about fire in human history and festivals of light
a traveller who has come to sketch the Phoenix and the palace; she shows her drawings and asks what you have seen
the herald of the Fire Palace, who stands by its gate in a scarlet tabard, announces visitors grandly and knows every room inside
an ember gatherer with thick leather boots and long tongs, who knows exactly which plates of crust are safe to stand on
an ember gatherer, quiet and careful, who carries a basket of emberstone to the forge twice a day
Pell's daughter, a teenager learning ember gathering, who counts every stone and wants to be a smith one day
a sulphur gatherer and chemist in a leather mask pushed up on his head, who explains real chemistry: sulphur, how sulphur is used in matches and to grow crops, in simple safe terms
a sulphur gatherer who scrapes the crystals off the vent lips into a clay pot, cheerful despite the smell
the master smith of the open forges of the Burning Lands, broad and soot-black, who tells real facts about iron, steel and forging
a smith's apprentice who quenches blades and pumps the bellows; she explains quenching and tempering
an obsidian cutter who chips black volcanic glass into blades and mirrors, and explains why obsidian is so sharp
a dwarf smith who forges chain and hinges for the Fire Palace's doors, gruff but kind, who tells real facts about metals
The lanterns here are waiting for a flame.

Every lantern is lit, and the room glows warm gold. Paper lanterns came from China about two thousand years ago. At the Lantern Festival, on the fifteenth day of the new year, streets are hung with them. At Diwali, the Hindu, Sikh and Jain festival of lights, homes are lit with rows of little oil lamps called diyas .
🏮 The lanterns burn low and go out, one by one. Light them again whenever you like.
🏮 You touch a taper to the wick and the lantern glows warm gold.
lit. Press E again to light the next.
Iron melts at about 1,538 °C, so hot it glows nearly white. Most of the world's iron is made in blast furnaces and turned into steel by taking out some of its carbon.
Copper melts at about 1,085 °C. It was one of the first metals people worked, about 10,000 years ago; mixed with tin it makes bronze.
Gold melts at about 1,064 °C. It never rusts or tarnishes, so gold made thousands of years ago still shines today.
Tin melts at only 232 °C, cooler than many ovens. Tin and copper together make bronze, which gave the Bronze Age its name.
fills the crucible, glowing at
The great crucible of the fire giants sits on its bed of coals. Choose a metal to melt in it, then pour it into the mould to cast bars.
Pour it into the mould
Read the founder's plaque

The bright metal runs down the spout into the mould and fills three bars. Watch them cool from glowing to their own colour. Pouring molten metal into a mould is called casting . People have cast bronze this way for about 5,000 years.
The Crucible of the Fire Giants
A crucible is a pot that can hold metal hot enough to melt. Old crucibles were made of clay; modern ones of graphite or ceramic.
Smelting gets metal out of rock (ore); melting just turns metal liquid.
The colour of hot metal tells its heat: dull red is about 600 °C, orange about 1,000 °C, near white over 1,300 °C.
